title: Toph Does Not Do Poetry
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 10 of 40
content:
Toph took another eleven days.

Nobody counted out loud.

This was because Toph threatened to bury anyone who did.

I did not push.

That was harder than it sounded.

After Aang and Katara kissed me, the shape of the relationship became visible in a way it had not been before. Aang could take my hand in the market. Katara could kiss my cheek before leaving for the clinic. People noticed. Some stared. Most decided the Avatar’s personal life was less interesting than whatever they were buying for dinner.

Toph acted exactly the same.

Which meant she insulted me constantly, invaded my office whenever she was bored, and once left a fist-sized chunk of polished meteorite on my desk with no explanation.

I found her at the metalbending school that evening.

Students had gone home. The courtyard was quiet except for the scrape of metal from the workshop.

Toph stood beside a forge shaping a narrow strip of steel without touching it. The metal bent in small, precise increments under her hands.

I waited until she finished.

“You left something on my desk.”

“No idea what you’re talking about.”

“It is literally a rock.”

“Sounds like office clutter.”

“It has been polished.”

“Fancy clutter.”

I held it out.

Toph did not reach for it.

“I don’t want it back.”

“I didn’t say you did.”

“Then why are you here?”

The question was sharper than necessary.

I lowered my hand.

“Because I wanted to say thank you.”

“You did.”

“And ask why.”

“There it is.”

Toph turned toward the open courtyard.

I followed.

The evening had gone cool. She sat on the edge of the training platform and let her feet rest against the packed earth below.

I sat beside her.

The meteorite stayed in my hand.

For a while she said nothing.

Then, “Sokka gave me a piece of one once.”

I knew the story only vaguely.

“He thought I’d like it because I could bend it,” she continued. “Metal from the sky. Weird stuff.”

“Did you?”

“Yeah.”

Her fingers tapped against her knee.

“I kept it.”

The meaning arrived slowly.

I looked at the stone in my hand.

“You gave me something like it.”

“Don’t make it dramatic.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re thinking dramatically.”

“You can’t sense thoughts.”

“I can sense the stupid breathing you do before saying something emotional.”

I shut my mouth.

Toph smiled.

“Better.”

The silence that followed was not uncomfortable.

That had become one of my favorite things about Toph. She did not require words to prove closeness. Sometimes she wanted to sit near someone and let the world stay quiet.

Then she said, “I don’t know how to do this.”

I turned toward her.

“Do what?”

She made an impatient gesture between us.

“This.”

“Dating?”

“Ugh.”

“Romance?”

“Worse.”

“Feelings?”

Toph groaned. “I’m leaving.”

I caught her wrist before she could stand.

She froze.

I immediately loosened my grip.

“Sorry.”

Toph did not pull away.

Instead she turned her hand and caught mine.

“I know how to fight people,” she said. “I know how to teach. I know how to tell when somebody’s lying. I know how to build things that don’t move.”

“Most of those seem useful.”

“Love moves.”

The words were so unexpectedly poetic that I stared.

Toph scowled.

“Say one thing.”

“I didn’t.”

“You thought it.”

“You said you can’t sense thoughts.”

“I can sense smug.”

I laughed.

Her thumb moved across my knuckles.

“I spent my whole childhood fighting people who thought love meant keeping me safe by keeping me small,” she said. “Then I ran away and found a bunch of idiots who cared about me without knowing how to shut up about it.”

“That sounds difficult.”

“It was.”

“And good?”

Toph was quiet.

“Yeah.”

I looked at our hands.

“What are you afraid I’ll do?”

“Decide I’m supposed to be softer because we’re together.”

“I like you like this.”

“I’m not finished.”

“Sorry.”

“Decide I’m supposed to need you. Decide you get to speak for me. Decide Katara’s better at the sweet stuff so I should copy her. Decide Aang’s better at saying feelings so I should copy him.”

Her grip tightened.

“Decide I’m bad at loving you because I don’t do it the way they do.”

That was the center of it.

I set the meteorite beside us.

“You don’t have to love me the way they do.”

Toph’s face turned toward mine.

“You don’t have to love me at all.”

Her brows drew together.

“I know.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

She stood.

For one alarming second I thought I had ruined it.

Then she pulled me up with her.

Toph was close enough that I could feel the heat of her body.

“I’m going to do something,” she said.

“Should I be worried?”

“Probably.”

“Helpful.”

Her hand lifted to my jaw.

Not delicate.

Careful, though.

Toph traced my face with her fingertips in a way she had never done before. Brow. Cheekbone. The line beside my mouth.

Her touch was not about seeing me the way sighted people did.

It was about knowing where I was.

Where we were.

My breath caught.

Toph smiled faintly.

“There’s the heartbeat.”

“Please don’t narrate this.”

“Bossy.”

“Toph.”

She kissed me.

No warning beyond the entire conversation.

Her mouth was warm and certain. The first kiss was brief, almost testing.

Then she kissed me again.

Harder.

One hand stayed at my jaw. The other caught my shirt near the waist and pulled me closer.

I laughed against her mouth.

Toph bit my lower lip lightly.

I stopped laughing.

She grinned.

“Cheater,” I whispered.

“There are no rules.”

“There should be.”

“Boring.”

I kissed her this time.

Toph went still for half a heartbeat.

Then softened.

Not into Katara.

Not into Aang.

Into herself.

Her forehead rested against mine when we separated.

The city hummed beyond the walls.

Metal cooled in the workshop behind us.

Toph’s hand remained at my waist.

“That was terrible,” she said.

“Awful.”

“Never again.”

“Obviously.”

She kissed me a third time.

When we finally sat back down, I picked up the meteorite.

“Can I keep this?”

Toph leaned back on her hands.

“Thought you’d never ask.”

I turned the stone over in my palm.

It had small ridges left from the shaping process. Not perfectly smooth. Not ornamental.

Toph had made it beautiful without making it delicate.

I understood the gift better now.

The next morning, Aang saw it on the cord around my neck.

His eyes widened.

Katara smiled immediately.

Toph walked in behind me and said, “Nobody say anything.”

Aang pressed both lips together.

Katara bit the inside of her cheek.

I lasted three seconds.

“She kissed me.”

Aang cheered.

Katara hugged Toph.

Toph threatened all of us with structural damage.

Later, while we ate breakfast, she hooked one bare foot around my ankle beneath the table.

She did not mention it.

Neither did I.

Toph did not do poetry.

She did pressure, presence, gifts made from impossible metal, and the steady weight of a foot against mine under the table.

I was learning to read her language.

A week later, I found another metal shape on my desk.

This one was not a flower.

It was a tiny four-pointed piece, each arm bent in a different direction. Crude by Toph’s standards, which meant it was only more precise than anything I could have made in a lifetime.

I carried it to the academy.

Toph was correcting a student’s stance by kicking their feet farther apart.

“You left something in my room.”

“Nope.”

I held it up.

She did not turn toward me. “Never seen it.”

“It has your fingerprints in the metal.”

“That is not how metal works.”

“I’m improvising.”

Her student looked between us with open fascination.

Toph pointed toward the far wall. “Twenty forms. Go.”

The student fled happily.

I sat on the edge of the practice platform. “What is it?”

Toph shrugged.

I waited.

Silence was one of the few tools that occasionally worked on her.

Finally she said, “Directions.”

“Four of them?”

“Don’t get sentimental.”

“I would never.”

“It’s just—” She scowled. “People keep talking like relationships are lines. One person, then another person. Somebody in front, somebody behind.”

I turned the metal piece in my fingers.

Toph continued, “Directions aren’t a line. You can face one without erasing the others.”

For a woman who did not do poetry, she was alarmingly bad at avoiding it.

I slipped the piece into my pocket.

“Thank you.”

“I didn’t make it.”

“Of course not.”

“And if you tell Katara I said that, I’ll deny it.”

“I thought you could tell when people lie.”

“I can. That’s why I know denial works if you commit.”

Her foot bumped mine.

I left it there.

Some love letters were written in ink.

Toph’s came forged from metal and plausible deniability.

I kept the metal directions in my pocket until the edges warmed from my body. Toph never admitted making them. I never asked her to.

The little piece stayed warm in my pocket all the way home.
